content_voiceover: When it comes to primary therapy for Waldenström macroglobulinemia, rituximab monotherapy alone is only modestly active, four doses give an overall response rate of twenty five to thirty percent, extending to eight doses raises that to forty to forty five percent, but deep responses are rare, with VGPR or CR under ten percent either way. Combining rituximab with other agents substantially improves both response rate and depth. Rituximab plus cyclophosphamide-based regimens, like CHOP-R, CVP-R, or CDR, achieve seventy to eighty percent overall response. Rituximab plus a nucleoside analog, such as fludarabine-rituximab or FCR, and rituximab plus a proteasome inhibitor like bortezomib, push overall response into the seventy to ninety percent range, with time to progression stretching out to five or six years for the proteasome inhibitor combinations. The best results come from rituximab plus bendamustine, with a ninety percent overall response rate, thirty to forty percent VGPR or CR, and a time to progression of sixty nine months, making it, along with the BTK inhibitor zanubrutinib, a preferred NCCN first-line regimen. One important exam pearl, rituximab alone can trigger an IgM flare that transiently worsens hyperviscosity, so in patients with very high IgM levels, plasmapheresis or holding rituximab initially should be considered before starting therapy.
keypoints: Rituximab monotherapy modest, ORR 25-45 percent, shallow response depth
Adding cyclophosphamide, nucleoside analog, or bortezomib raises ORR to 70-90 percent
Bendamustine-rituximab is preferred: ORR 90 percent, VGPR/CR 30-40 percent, TTP 69 months
Watch for rituximab-induced IgM flare worsening hyperviscosity in high IgM patients
keypoint_voiceover: Key takeaways are that bendamustine-rituximab and zanubrutinib are the preferred first-line options, combination therapy far outperforms rituximab alone, and IgM flare is a real risk to anticipate before treating high-IgM patients.
